claim: PL35 family glycosaminoglycan lyases have an ultrabroad substrate spectrum that can degrade three types of uronic acid-containing GAGs (hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulfate and heparan sulfate) or even alginate.
source: Recently, a new class of glycosaminoglycan (GAG) lyases (GAGases) belonging to PL35 family has been discovered with an ultrabroad substrate spectrum that can degrade three types of uronic acid-containing GAGs (hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulfate and heparan sulfate) or even alginate.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous experimental characterization of PL35 family enzymes and is cited in the abstract.

claim: The structure of GAGase II from Spirosoma fluviale was determined at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: The structures of GAGase II from Spirosoma fluviale (GenBank accession number: SOD82962.1, 81.2% sequence identity with GAGase I), GAGase VII from Bacteroides intestinalis (GenBank accession number: EDV05210.1, 44.8% sequence identity with GAGase I) and selenomethionine (SeMet)-labeled GAGase II (Se-GAGase II) in their ligand-free states were solved at 1.9 Å, 2.4 Å, and 2.0 Å resolution, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: The resolution is directly stated and supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The structure of GAGase VII from Bacteroides intestinalis was determined at 2.4 Å resolution.
source: The structures of GAGase II from Spirosoma fluviale (GenBank accession number: SOD82962.1, 81.2% sequence identity with GAGase I), GAGase VII from Bacteroides intestinalis (GenBank accession number: EDV05210.1, 44.8% sequence identity with GAGase I) and selenomethionine (SeMet)-labeled GAGase II (Se-GAGase II) in their ligand-free states were solved at 1.9 Å, 2.4 Å, and 2.0 Å resolution, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: The resolution is directly stated and supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: GAGase II and GAGase VII consist of an N-terminal (α/α)6 toroid multidomain and a C-terminal two-layered β-sheet domain with Mn2+.
source: Structural analysis showed that GAGase II and GAGase VII consist of an N-terminal (α/α)6 toroid multidomain and a C-terminal two-layered β-sheet domain with Mn2+.
evidence: This structural description is based on the crystal structures determined in this study and confirmed by ICP-MS analysis for metal identification.

claim: GAGases exhibit higher structural similarity with alginate lyases than GAG lyases.
source: Notably, although GAGases share similar folds and catalytic mechanisms with some GAG lyases and alginate lyases, they exhibit higher structural similarity with alginate lyases than GAG lyases, which may present a crucial structural evidence for the speculation that GAG lyases with (α/α)n toroid and antiparallel β-sheet structures arrived by a divergent evolution from alginate lyases with the same folds.
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment data presented in Tables 2 and 3 showing RMSD values and Z-scores.

claim: GAG lyases with (α/α)n toroid and antiparallel β-sheet structures may have arrived by divergent evolution from alginate lyases with the same folds.
source: Notably, although GAGases share similar folds and catalytic mechanisms with some GAG lyases and alginate lyases, they exhibit higher structural similarity with alginate lyases than GAG lyases, which may present a crucial structural evidence for the speculation that GAG lyases with (α/α)n toroid and antiparallel β-sheet structures arrived by a divergent evolution from alginate lyases with the same folds.
evidence: This evolutionary hypothesis is supported by structural similarity data and is presented as speculation based on the structural evidence.

claim: GAGs are linear polyanionic polysaccharides ubiquitously distributed on the cell surface and in the extracellular matrix (ECM) of animal tissues.
source: GAGs are a class of linear polyanionic polysaccharides ubiquitously distributed on the cell surface and in the extracellular matrix (ECM) of animal tissues (Cohen and Merzendorfer, 2019), and they participate in various physiological and pathological processes through interacting with a series of chemokines (Dyer et al., 2016; Irie et al., 2008), growth factors (Sirko et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2019) or other ECM components.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: GAGs participate in various physiological and pathological processes through interacting with chemokines, growth factors, or other ECM components.
source: GAGs are a class of linear polyanionic polysaccharides ubiquitously distributed on the cell surface and in the extracellular matrix (ECM) of animal tissues (Cohen and Merzendorfer, 2019), and they participate in various physiological and pathological processes through interacting with a series of chemokines (Dyer et al., 2016; Irie et al., 2008), growth factors (Sirko et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2019) or other ECM components.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Except for keratan sulfate (KS), other GAGs are composed of repeating disaccharides consisting of hexuronic acid (HexUA) and hexosamine (HexNAc).
source: Except for keratan sulfate (KS), which does not contain hexuronic acid (HexUA) residues, other GAGs are composed of repeating disaccharides consisting of HexUA (d-glucuronic acid (GlcUA) or l-iduronic acid (IdoUA)) and hexosamine (HexNAc) (d-N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) or d-N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc)).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GAG structure.

claim: HexUA-containing GAGs are classified into three classes: hyaluronan (HA), chondroitin sulfate (CS)/dermatan sulfate (DS) and heparan sulfate (HS)/heparin (Hep).
source: Based on the disaccharide composition and the type of glycosidic bonds between disaccharides units, HexUA-containing GAGs are classified into three classes: hyaluronan (HA), chondroitin sulfate (CS)/dermatan sulfate (DS) and heparan sulfate (HS)/heparin (Hep) (Cohen and Merzendorfer, 2019).
evidence: This classification is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HA is the only non-sulfated GAG composed of repeating -GlcUAβ1-3GlcNAc- disaccharides linked by β1–4 glycosidic bonds.
source: HA is the only non-sulfated GAG composed of repeating -GlcUAβ1-3GlcNAc- disaccharides linked by β1–4 glycosidic bonds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HA structure.

claim: The backbone of CS is composed of repeating -GlcUAβ1-3GalNAc- disaccharides linked by β1–4 glycosidic bonds.
source: The backbone of CS is composed of repeating -GlcUAβ1-3GalNAc- disaccharides linked by β1–4 glycosidic bonds, and is further sulfated at C-2 of GlcUA and C-4/C-6 of GalNAc by sulfotransferases; meanwhile, the GlcUA residues in CS can be epimerized into IdoUA residues by glucuronyl C-5 epimerase to form DS (Kusche-Gullberg and Kjellén, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CS structure supported by citation.

claim: GAG lyases specifically catalyze the degradation of HexUA-containing GAGs via a β-elimination mechanism.
source: GAG lyases, belonging to the superfamily of polysaccharide lyases (PLs), specifically catalyze the degradation of HexUA-containing GAGs (Charnock et al., 2002; Garron and Cygler, 2010). These reactions generate a plethora of oligosaccharides that contain an unsaturated double bond between C-4 and C-5 on uronic acids at their nonreducing ends, which is generated via a β-elimination mechanism (Garron and Cygler, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GAG lyase mechanism supported by citations.

claim: GAG lyases degrade HexUA-containing GAGs without the participation of a water molecule.
source: As a complimentary mechanistic strategy to glycoside hydrolases (GHs), GAG lyases degrade HexUA-containing GAGs without the participation of a water molecule and are involved in the polysaccharide metabolism of microorganisms (Garron and Cygler, 2010; Ndeh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GAG lyase mechanism supported by citations.

claim: 44 families (and an unclassified PL0 family) of polysaccharide lyases have been hierarchically classified in the CAZy database.
source: Based on their sequence similarity, 44 families (and an unclassified PL0 family) have been hierarchically classified in the CAZy database (http://www.cazy.org/), and at least one member of each family has been subjected to activity identification and biochemical property analysis (Drula et al., 2022).
evidence: This is factual information about the CAZy database classification supported by citation.

claim: Identified GAG lyases are widely distributed in the PL6, PL8, PL12, PL13, PL15, PL16, PL21, PL23, PL29, PL30, PL33, PL35, and PL37 families.
source: The identified GAG lyases are widely distributed in the PL6, PL8, PL12, PL13, PL15, PL16, PL21, PL23, PL29, PL30, PL33, PL35, and PL37 families (Drula et al., 2022).
evidence: This is factual information about GAG lyase classification supported by citation.

claim: All identified GAG lyases have substrate specificity to strictly distinguish one or two kinds of GAGs based on saccharide composition and glycosidic bonds.
source: All identified GAG lyases have substrate specificity to strictly distinguish one or two kinds of GAGs based on saccharide composition and glycosidic bonds between each HexUA-HexNAc disaccharide units, while other uronic acid-containing polysaccharides are usually unable to serve as substrates for these enzymes.
evidence: This is a generalization based on established knowledge of GAG lyase specificity.

claim: Alginate is an unbranched anionic extracellular polysaccharide produced by lower organisms algae and bacteria.
source: As a kind of unbranched anionic extracellular polysaccharide produced by lower organisms algae and bacteria such as brown alga (Popper et al., 2011) and bacteria belonging to Pseudomonas (Evans and Linker, 1973) and Azotobacter (Clementi, 1997), alginate containing no hexosamine and sulfation possesses a simpler structure than GAGs in animals and likely emerge earlier than GAGs during the course of evolution.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Alginate possesses a simpler structure than GAGs in animals and likely emerged earlier than GAGs during the course of evolution.
source: As a kind of unbranched anionic extracellular polysaccharide produced by lower organisms algae and bacteria such as brown alga (Popper et al., 2011) and bacteria belonging to Pseudomonas (Evans and Linker, 1973) and Azotobacter (Clementi, 1997), alginate containing no hexosamine and sulfation possesses a simpler structure than GAGs in animals and likely emerge earlier than GAGs during the course of evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural complexity and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Alginate is composed of d-mannuronate (M) and its C5 epimer l-guluronate (G).
source: Like GAGs, alginate is a linear polyanionic polysaccharide that contains HexUA residues; however, alginate possesses a completely different chemical structure, which is composed of d-mannuronate (M) and its C5 epimer l-guluronate (G), and M and G residues often alternate randomly to form heteropolyuronic blocks, including polyM composed of M residues linked by β1–4 bonds, polyG composed of G residues linked by α1–4 bonds, and polyMG/GM composed of alternating M and G linked by β/α1–4 bonds (Pawar and Edgar, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about alginate structure supported by citation.

claim: Alginate lyases belong to the PL5, PL6, PL7, PL8, PL14, PL15, PL17, PL18, PL31, PL32, PL34, PL36, PL38, PL39, PL41, and PL44 families.
source: Likewise, a series of alginate lyases essential for the metabolism of alginate were identified from microorganisms and algae as well as lower marine animals, which belong to the PL5, PL6, PL7, PL8, PL14, PL15, PL17, PL18, PL31, PL32, PL34, PL36, PL38, PL39, PL41, and PL44 families (Drula et al., 2022).
evidence: This is factual information about alginate lyase classification supported by citation.

claim: GAG lyases are thought to have originated from alginate lyases by divergent evolution through adaptation to the evolution of substrate polysaccharides.
source: From an evolutionary perspective in previous reports, GAG lyases are thought to have originated from alginate lyases by a divergent evolution through adaptation to the evolution of substrate polysaccharides.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature presented as established speculation.

claim: The (α/α)n toroid and antiparallel β-sheet folds of GAG lyases are found in families such as PL8, PL12, PL21, and PL23.
source: For example, the (α/α)n toroid and antiparallel β-sheet folds of GAG lyases are found in families such as PL8 (hyaluronate lyase and chondroitin lyase), PL12 (heparinase III), PL21 (heparinase II), and PL23 (chondroitin lyase).
evidence: This is established knowledge about structural folds in GAG lyases.

claim: Alginate lyases in PL15, PL17, and PL39 families exhibit (α/α)n toroid and antiparallel β-sheet folds.
source: Alginate lyases in PL15, PL17, and PL39 families also exhibit these folds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about structural folds in alginate lyases.

claim: GAGase III can degrade alginate in addition to GAGs.
source: More interestingly, one of the eight identified GAGases (GAGase III) can even degrade alginate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: GAGases selectively act on GAG domains composed of non/6-O-/N-sulfated hexosamines and d-glucuronic acid.
source: Analysis of substrate structure preference represented by GAGase I showed that GAGases selectively act on GAG domains composed of non/6-O-/N-sulfated hexosamines and d-glucuronic acid, among which GAGase III can also selectively degrade polyM blocks composed of d-mannuronic acids but not polyG blocks composed of l-guluronic acids in alginate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: GAGase III can selectively degrade polyM blocks composed of d-mannuronic acids but not polyG blocks composed of l-guluronic acids in alginate.
source: Analysis of substrate structure preference represented by GAGase I showed that GAGases selectively act on GAG domains composed of non/6-O-/N-sulfated hexosamines and d-glucuronic acid, among which GAGase III can also selectively degrade polyM blocks composed of d-mannuronic acids but not polyG blocks composed of l-guluronic acids in alginate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: GAGases have considerable degree of similarity with GAG lyases from PL15, PL21, and PL33 families and alginate lyases from PL15, PL17, and PL34 families.
source: Furthermore, the primary structure alignment and phylogenetic analysis showed that GAGases have considerable degree of similarity with not only GAG lyases from PL15, PL21, and PL33 families but also alginate lyases from PL15, PL17, and PL34 families (Wei et al., 2024), indicating that GAGases may exhibit some transitional features from alginate lyases to GAG lyases in structure.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis data from previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: GAGases may exhibit some transitional features from alginate lyases to GAG lyases in structure.
source: Furthermore, the primary structure alignment and phylogenetic analysis showed that GAGases have considerable degree of similarity with not only GAG lyases from PL15, PL21, and PL33 families but also alginate lyases from PL15, PL17, and PL34 families (Wei et al., 2024), indicating that GAGases may exhibit some transitional features from alginate lyases to GAG lyases in structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence and structural similarity data.

claim: Both GAGase II and GAGase VII are monomers consisting of two domains: an N-terminal (α/α)6 toroid domain and a C-terminal two-layered β-sheet domain.
source: Both GAGase II and GAGase VII are monomers consisting of two domains: an N-terminal (α/α)6 toroid domain and a C-terminal two-layered β-sheet domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The N-terminal domain (Met34-Ala365) of GAGase II is composed of 16 large or small α-helices (α1-α16) to form an (α/α)6 toroid domain.
source: The N-terminal domain (Met34-Ala365) of GAGase II is composed of 16 large or small α-helices (α1-α16) to form an (α/α)6 toroid domain.
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure of GAGase II.

claim: The C-terminal domain (Met366-Ser612) of GAGase II is composed of 17 β-strands (β1-β17) to form a two-layered β-sheet domain with four small α-helices.
source: The C-terminal domain (Met366-Ser612) of GAGase II is composed of 17 β-strands (β1-β17) to form a two-layered β-sheet domain with four small α-helices located between β5-β6 and β8-β9.
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure of GAGase II.

claim: A Mn2+ was detected in C-terminal domains of both GAGase II and VII by ICP-MS analysis.
source: Unlike the GAG lyases identified from PL8, PL15, and PL21 families, which contain Ca2+ or Zn2+ in their overall crystal structures (Shaya et al., 2008b; Shaya et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2021), a Mn2+ was detected in C-terminal domains of both GAGase II and VII by inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) analysis (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by ICP-MS experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1b and visualized in Figure 1B.

claim: The Mn2+ is located inside the long Ω loop after the β1-β5 antiparallel β-sheet and coordinates with nearby nitrogen and oxygen atoms of several residues such as Asp and His.
source: Structurally, the Mn2+ is located inside the long Ω loop after the β1-β5 antiparallel β-sheet, and coordinates with the nearby nitrogen and oxygen atoms of several residues such as Asp and His in both GAGase VII and GAGase II (GAGase II also has coordination with three surrounding water molecules), with distances of 2.0–2.5 Å.
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structures.

claim: Mutation of His403, Asp405, Asp421, and His457 in GAGase II to alanine resulted in complete or substantial inactivation of GAGase II.
source: To investigate the roles of these adjacent residues interacting with the Mn2+, His403, Asp405, Asp421, and His457 in GAGase II were individually mutated to alanine (Ala), and the results showed that these variants resulted in complete or substantial inactivation of GAGase II (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EDTA inhibits and Mn2+ stimulates the enzymatic activities of GAGases.
source: In addition, the inhibitory effects of the chelator (EDTA) and the stimulation of Mn2+ on the enzymatic activities also support the critical role of Mn2+ on GAGases (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GAGase II shares 23.1% sequence identity with PL21 heparinase II from Pedobacter heparinus.
source: Notably, GAGase II shares very low sequence identity with PL21 heparinase II from Pedobacter heparinus (Shaya et al., 2006) (23.1% identity with 29% query coverage), PL12 heparinase III from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicronin (Ulaganathan et al., 2017) (23.6% identity with 32% query cover) and PL39 alginate lyase from Defluviitalea phaphyphila (Ji et al., 2019) (26.5% identity with 31% coverage), and no significant sequence identity with PL17 alginate lyases (Park et al., 2014), PL15 exoHep (Zhang et al., 2021), PL8 chondroitin ABC lyase (Shaya et al., 2008a) and chondroitin AC lyase Lunin et al., 2004; however, all are relatively well superimposable in their overall structures and highly conserved in their triplet active site residues (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: GAGase II shares 23.6% sequence identity with PL12 heparinase III from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicronin.
source: Notably, GAGase II shares very low sequence identity with PL21 heparinase II from Pedobacter heparinus (Shaya et al., 2006) (23.1% identity with 29% query coverage), PL12 heparinase III from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicronin (Ulaganathan et al., 2017) (23.6% identity with 32% query cover) and PL39 alginate lyase from Defluviitalea phaphyphila (Ji et al., 2019) (26.5% identity with 31% coverage), and no significant sequence identity with PL17 alginate lyases (Park et al., 2014), PL15 exoHep (Zhang et al., 2021), PL8 chondroitin ABC lyase (Shaya et al., 2008a) and chondroitin AC lyase Lunin et al., 2004; however, all are relatively well superimposable in their overall structures and highly conserved in their triplet active site residues (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: GAGase II shares 26.5% sequence identity with PL39 alginate lyase from Defluviitalea phaphyphila.
source: Notably, GAGase II shares very low sequence identity with PL21 heparinase II from Pedobacter heparinus (Shaya et al., 2006) (23.1% identity with 29% query coverage), PL12 heparinase III from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicronin (Ulaganathan et al., 2017) (23.6% identity with 32% query cover) and PL39 alginate lyase from Defluviitalea phaphyphila (Ji et al., 2019) (26.5% identity with 31% coverage), and no significant sequence identity with PL17 alginate lyases (Park et al., 2014), PL15 exoHep (Zhang et al., 2021), PL8 chondroitin ABC lyase (Shaya et al., 2008a) and chondroitin AC lyase Lunin et al., 2004; however, all are relatively well superimposable in their overall structures and highly conserved in their triplet active site residues (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: GAGase II has no significant sequence identity with PL17 alginate lyases, PL15 exoHep, PL8 chondroitin ABC lyase and chondroitin AC lyase, but all are relatively well superimposable in their overall structures.
source: Notably, GAGase II shares very low sequence identity with PL21 heparinase II from Pedobacter heparinus (Shaya et al., 2006) (23.1% identity with 29% query coverage), PL12 heparinase III from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicronin (Ulaganathan et al., 2017) (23.6% identity with 32% query cover) and PL39 alginate lyase from Defluviitalea phaphyphila (Ji et al., 2019) (26.5% identity with 31% coverage), and no significant sequence identity with PL17 alginate lyases (Park et al., 2014), PL15 exoHep (Zhang et al., 2021), PL8 chondroitin ABC lyase (Shaya et al., 2008a) and chondroitin AC lyase Lunin et al., 2004; however, all are relatively well superimposable in their overall structures and highly conserved in their triplet active site residues (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The (α/α)n toroid domain and anti-parallel β-sheet domain of GAGase II show more structural similarity to alginate lyases from PL15, PL17, and PL39 families than various GAG lyases.
source: In terms of overall structural similarities, the (α/α)n toroid domain and anti-parallel β-sheet domain of GAGase II show more structural similarity to alginate lyases with (α/α)6 toroid and the antiparallel β-sheet domain, such as those from the PL15 (PDB code: 3A0O) (Ochiai et al., 2010), PL17 (PDB code: 4NEI) (Park et al., 2014), and PL39 (PDB code: 6JP4) (Ji et al., 2019) families, than various GAG lyases (Tables 2 and 3), indicating that GAGases might have originated from alginate lyases rather than GAG lyases.
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment data in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: GAGases might have originated from alginate lyases rather than GAG lyases.
source: In terms of overall structural similarities, the (α/α)n toroid domain and anti-parallel β-sheet domain of GAGase II show more structural similarity to alginate lyases with (α/α)6 toroid and the antiparallel β-sheet domain, such as those from the PL15 (PDB code: 3A0O) (Ochiai et al., 2010), PL17 (PDB code: 4NEI) (Park et al., 2014), and PL39 (PDB code: 6JP4) (Ji et al., 2019) families, than various GAG lyases (Tables 2 and 3), indicating that GAGases might have originated from alginate lyases rather than GAG lyases.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity data.

claim: The conserved residues Tyr246, His401, Asn192 of GAGase II, Tyr243, His398, Asn189 of GAGase III, and Tyr241, His397, Asn187 of GAGase VII may be the key triplet residues involved in β-elimination catalysis.
source: Based on the sequence and structural alignment with homogenous alginate/GAG lyases, the conserved residues Tyr246, His401, Asn192 of GAGase II, Tyr243, His398, Asn189 of GAGase III, and Tyr241, His397, Asn187 of GAGase VII may be the key triplet residues involved in β-elimination catalysis (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural alignment with known lyases shown in Figure 3.

claim: Individual mutation of Tyr246, His401, Asn192 in GAGase II to Ala resulted in complete loss of activity toward CS-C.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, these residues were individually replaced by Ala and the activity of the mutants was analyzed. The results showed that the activity of all variants toward CS-C was completely lost (Figure 4A), indicating that GAGases act through a general acid-base catalytic mechanism by using His/Tyr as a Brønsted acid/base, similar to that observed for various other identified GAG/alginate lyases (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GAGases act through a general acid-base catalytic mechanism by using His/Tyr as a Brønsted acid/base.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, these residues were individually replaced by Ala and the activity of the mutants was analyzed. The results showed that the activity of all variants toward CS-C was completely lost (Figure 4A), indicating that GAGases act through a general acid-base catalytic mechanism by using His/Tyr as a Brønsted acid/base, similar to that observed for various other identified GAG/alginate lyases (Table 4).
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis data and comparison with known lyases.

claim: GAGase II contains a shorter catalytic cavity compared to structurally similar GAG/alginate lyases.
source: Compared with structurally similar GAG/alginate lyases, the results from molecular docking and catalytic tunnel predictions showed that GAGase II contains a shorter catalytic cavity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which may explain why they can accommodate and degrade a variety of substrates with very different structures.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and tunnel prediction shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The shorter catalytic cavity of GAGase II may explain why they can accommodate and degrade a variety of substrates with very different structures.
source: Compared with structurally similar GAG/alginate lyases, the results from molecular docking and catalytic tunnel predictions showed that GAGase II contains a shorter catalytic cavity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which may explain why they can accommodate and degrade a variety of substrates with very different structures.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on structural observations.

claim: The nonreducing end of the HA hexasaccharide substrate at the '–1' and '–2' subsites is near positively charged amino acids including Arg87, Arg88, Arg94, His136, Asn191 and Asn192 in GAGase II.
source: Based on the docking results obtained for GAGase II with an HA Hexa (GlcUA1–3GlcNAc)3 (PDB code: 1HYA) (Winter et al., 1975; Figure 4B), the nonreducing end of the substrate at the '–1' and '–2' subsites is near some positively charged amino acids, including Arg87, Arg88, Arg94, His136, Asn191 and Asn192, in the vicinity of the catalytic cavity of GAGase II, which could facilitate the binding of negatively charged substrates.
evidence: This is based on molecular docking results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Several acidic amino acids (Glu242, Asp299, and Glu431) are very close to the '+1' and '+2' subsites in GAGase II, which could promote the release of the reducing end product via charge repulsion.
source: Besides, several acidic amino acids (Glu242, Asp299, and Glu431) are very close to the '+1' and '+2' subsites, which could promote the release of the reducing end product via charge repulsion.
evidence: This is based on molecular docking results and structural analysis.

claim: Site-directed mutagenesis of residues Tyr240, Gln307, Arg342, Tyr427, Glu428, Glu431, Trp438, Met440, and Arg446 in GAGase II resulted in partial or complete inactivation.
source: There are some other residues surrounding around the catalytic cavity, such as Tyr240, Gln307, Arg342, Tyr427, Glu428, Glu431, Trp438, Met440, and Arg446, which may play a key role in stabilization of the catalytic cavity and overall structure. Site-directed mutagenesis of these residues individually replaced with Ala showed that resulting variants were partially or completely inactivated (Figure 4C), confirming that these residues play important roles in the binding and release of substrate and structural stabilization.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GAGase III has a unique His188 residue in its catalytic cavity, which is conserved in alginate lyases from PL17, PL39, PL38, PL5, and PL15 families.
source: To investigate the reason why this enzyme is capable to act on alginate, its structure was predicted using RoseTTAfold, and aligned with GAGase II and GAGase VII. Results showed that GAGase III has a unique His188 residue in its catalytic cavity, which is conserved in alginate lyases from PL17 (Park et al., 2014), PL39 (Ji et al., 2019), PL38 (Rønne et al., 2023), PL5 (Pandey et al., 2021), and PL15 (Ochiai et al., 2010) families, while other GAGases have a conserved asparagine residue such as the Asn191 of GAGase II and the Asn186 of GAGase VII in the corresponding position (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is based on structural prediction and alignment shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The His188 residue is essential for the alginate-degrading activity of GAGase III.
source: To verify the function of this histidine, His188 was replaced with alanine and asparagine, respectively. The results of substrate-specificity analysis showed that the alginate-degrading activity of both GAGase III-H188A and GAGase III-H188N were abolished even at a quite high ratio of the mutated enzyme to substrate such as 30 μg enzyme to 30 μg substrate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), while their GAG-degrading activity was only partially affected, indicating that the His188 residue is essential for the alginate-degrading activity of GAGase III (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5C-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutation of the asparagine residue at the corresponding position of other GAGases to histidine did not confer alginate-degrading activity.
source: However, when the asparagine residue at the corresponding position of other GAGases was mutated to histidine, the obtained variants did not exhibit any alginate-degrading activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that degrading activity of GAGase II remains to be determined outside of the His188 residue.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GAGases prefer to degrade CS domains composed of non-/6-O-sulfated but not 4-O-sulfated GalNAc residues and d-GlcA residues.
